difaa19380707.note: The hospital-by-hospital tally printed the day after the Haifa market bombing of 6 July 1938. The register holds 34 injury admissions that day, of which one died — a 12-year-old Muslim boy with a bullet wound to chest and abdomen, admitted 6 July, died 7 July. 34 − 1 = 33, exactly the paper's count.
difaa19380707.orig: في مستشفى الحكومة: ٣٣ مصاباً بينهم ٧ في حالة خطرة
difaa19380707.trans: In the Government Hospital: 33 injured, among them 7 in critical condition.

difaa19460822.note: The one attestation that places the kerentina inside the hospital rather than beside it. Read against Filastin of 11 September 1941, which names the hospital, the health offices and the Kerentina as three distinct things, this is likelier loose usage — someone calling the hospital's own Isolation department “the quarantine.” See §08.
difaa19460822.orig: الى الكرنتينا في مستشفى الحكومة بحيفا
difaa19460822.trans: …to the quarantine in the Government Hospital in Haifa.

difaa19470507.note: The register has a man of 20 admitted 5 May 1947 and dead on 6 May, “Punc. W. Abdomen (Oper.) Bowel Injury”, notebook 31 page 33 — one of eleven Jewish men aged 17–33 with gunshot wounds after the Acre citadel prison break. Same day, same place, same outcome. The press supplies a name the register's redaction removed.
difaa19470507.orig: توفي في مستشفى الحكومة بحيفا صباح امس ارهابي جريح يدعى نسيم عبادي
difaa19470507.trans: There died in the Government Hospital in Haifa yesterday morning a wounded terrorist named Nasim ʿAbbadi.

mb19400308.note: Tuesday evening is 5 March 1940. Notebook 24 ends on 1 March 1940 and nothing resumes until Notebook 29 on 8 February 1944, so this death falls four days inside the register's gap and cannot be checked against it at all. That is the point of it: it establishes from outside that the hospital was admitting patients and its deaths were being reported — which means the missing notebooks are missing, not never-written. Jüdische Weltrundschau carries the same event on 11 March.
mb19400308.orig: Am Dienstag abend starb im Regierungskrankenhaus in Haifa Lipmann Lipschitz, ein 27-jähriger aus Lettland stammender Jude, an den Verletzungen, die er bei der Demonstration erlitten hatte. An dem Begräbnis am Mittwoch nahmen unabsehbare Menschenmassen teil.
mb19400308.pub: Mitteilungsblatt der Hitachdut Olej Germania we Austria
mb19400308.trans: On Tuesday evening Lipmann Lipschitz, a 27-year-old Jew originally from Latvia, died in the Government Hospital in Haifa of the injuries he suffered at the demonstration. Immense crowds attended the burial on Wednesday.

mb19480123.id: MB, 23 January 1948, p.4 — “Haifaer Notizen”, datelined Haifa 11.1.48
mb19480123.note:
The same notice records Haifa short of 400 beds, a 70–80 bed emergency hospital opening in the Kupath Cholim rest home in Achuza, and sick and wounded lying in tents outside the Rothschild.

The register confirms it to the month: Jewish admissions run at 20, 59, 12, 26 and 35 a month through 1947, then 1 in January 1948, 2 in February, 0 in March, 0 in April. The Hebrew dailies supply the date and the cause — the walkout of 31 December 1947 (§09).
mb19480123.orig: Gleichzeitig mussten aus Sicherheitsgründen die jüdischen Kranken aus dem Regierungskrankenhaus herausgenommen werden!
mb19480123.trans: At the same time the Jewish patients had to be removed from the Government Hospital for security reasons.

wdt19260415.note: The Borromean Sisters' hospital tells its own history in the Templer weekly: the sisters took over a pilgrim house in 1888 and ran a poor-dispensary; in 1898 they rented a neighbouring house that had served the Templer community as schoolhouse and prayer hall, later buying and enlarging it when the Hejaz railway brought sick European labourers. Dr Peters directed it to 1913, then Dr Wilhelm Hoffmann, a grandson of the Templer colony's founder. Admissions rose from 155 in 1899 to 760 in 1925. It served the German communities of Haifa, Waldheim and Bethlehem of Galilee first, but was “fast immer überfüllt.”
